A purpose-built stack lets S3 optimize every layer for object storage specifically, such as heat-aware placement across millions of drives, at the cost of building and verifying more itself. Remember the caveat from earlier: even GCS's strong consistency has scope limits, since public caches and IAM permission changes remain eventually consistent.

quiz.q: Why does keeping GCS metadata in Spanner fit its strong consistency?
quiz.a: Spanner is a globally consistent database, so keeping object metadata there naturally gives strong consistency for reads, deletes and listings.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
title: Azure storage stamps: 2 PB to 30 PB clusters, kept near 70% full
body: Microsoft published the architecture of Windows Azure Storage, or WAS, at SOSP 2011, and it remains the clearest public design of a cloud object store. Its basic unit is the storage stamp, a cluster of racks. First-generation stamps held about 2 PB raw; the next generation held up to 30 PB. Microsoft aims to keep each stamp around 70% utilized and moves accounts between stamps as one fills up. A Location Service maps each storage account to a stamp.
deeper: The stamp is a unit of scale and failure. Instead of one giant global cluster, Azure builds many bounded clusters, each with its own full stack of front ends, partition servers and storage. That caps the blast radius of problems and makes capacity planning concrete: add stamps to grow. Keeping stamps near 70% utilization leaves headroom for bursts, drive failures and rebuilds, and for accepting accounts migrated from fuller stamps. The Location Service is what makes stamps invisible to customers. It maps each storage account to a stamp and updates DNS so that a name like account.blob.core.windows.net resolves to the right stamp. Moving an account between stamps therefore changes a DNS entry rather than every client's configuration. This contrasts with S3's approach of spreading each bucket's objects over a very large number of drives across the fleet. Azure's stamps bound an account to one cluster, while replication to another stamp provides geo disaster recovery. The next card covers what runs inside a stamp: the front-end, partition and stream layers.

quiz.q: How can Azure move a storage account between stamps without client changes?
quiz.a: The Location Service maps accounts to stamps and updates DNS, so the account's hostname simply points to the new stamp.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
title: Inside an Azure stamp: front end, partitions, streams
body: Each Azure stamp has three layers. Stateless front-end servers authenticate requests and route them to the right partition server. The partition layer manages blobs, tables and queues in range partitions, each served by one partition server; this is where strong consistency and per-partition transactions come from. The stream layer is an append-only distributed filesystem storing data in extents. An extent grows until it reaches a target size, is then sealed, and a sealed extent is immutable.
deeper: The layering mirrors S3's split of front end, index and storage. The front end is stateless and scales with requests. The partition layer is the metadata and consistency brain: because each range partition is served by a single partition server at a time, that server can order operations on its keys and offer strong consistency and transactions within the partition without distributed locking. The stream layer handles durability and bytes, knowing nothing about blobs or tables, just append-only streams of extents. Sealing is the key trick. While an extent is open for appends it is replicated synchronously within the stamp for durability. Once sealed, it can never change, which means the stream layer can later erasure code cold sealed extents to save space, exactly the immutability benefit described at the start of the chapter: parity is computed once and never updated. The chapter's in-industry note calls out that this seal-then-erasure-code approach is the same idea as Meta's hot in Haystack, then move to f4. Replication details are covered on the next card.

quiz.q: Why can Azure erasure code an extent only after it is sealed?
quiz.a: A sealed extent is immutable, so parity is computed once and never recalculated. Open extents are still being appended to.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
title: Azure replication: sync inside a stamp, async across regions
body: Windows Azure Storage uses two kinds of replication with different jobs. Intra-stamp replication, inside the stream layer, is synchronous: a write is copied to replicas within the stamp before it is acknowledged, which provides durability. Inter-stamp replication copies data to another stamp, typically in another region, asynchronously, which provides geographic disaster recovery. Splitting replication this way keeps write latency low while still protecting against the loss of an entire site.
deeper: Synchronous replication across regions would force every write to wait for a round trip over long distances, adding significant latency to every request. By keeping synchronous replication within a stamp, where replicas are close, Azure acknowledges writes quickly while still guaranteeing that an acknowledged write survives individual failures inside the cluster. Asynchronous replication to another stamp in another region handles the rarer, larger disaster: losing a whole stamp or site. The trade-off is that asynchronous copies lag slightly behind, so a sudden regional disaster could lose the most recent writes that had not yet been shipped. Within the stamp, the stream layer can also later erasure code cold sealed extents, reducing the storage overhead of synchronous replicas for data that is no longer changing. The chapter's comparison table summarizes Azure's data protection as synchronous replicas in the stamp, erasure coding of sealed extents, and asynchronous geo replication. Compare with Dropbox Magic Pocket, which stores each block in at least two geographic zones with cross-zone replication within about one second of upload.

quiz.q: Why is Azure's inter-stamp replication asynchronous rather than synchronous?
quiz.a: Synchronous cross-region copies would add long round trips to every write. Async geo replication keeps writes fast while still enabling disaster recovery.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
title: The universal pattern: metadata layer over immutable data
body: Look across S3, Windows Azure Storage and Colossus and the same pattern appears: a separate metadata or index layer sits over an append-only or immutable data layer, with erasure coding applied once data is sealed. The Azure paper's seal then erasure code is the same idea as Meta's hot in Haystack, then move to f4. Different companies converged on this architecture because it separates the hard coordination problem from the bulk byte-storage problem.
deeper: Why does this split keep winning? Metadata operations need consistency, ordering and fast lookups, but they involve small records. Data operations involve huge volumes of bytes but, if the data is immutable, need almost no coordination. Separating the two lets each layer use the right tools: a sharded index, Bigtable, Spanner, a partition layer or ZippyDB for metadata, and simple append-only storage for bytes. Immutable data also makes durability cheaper over time. New data is often kept in a form that is fast to write and read, such as replicas, while it is hot and still being assembled. Once sealed, it can be converted to an erasure-coded form with much lower overhead, because parity is computed once and never updated. The same arc shows up at Azure with sealed extents, Meta moving from Haystack's 3.6x replication to f4's 2.1x, and Dropbox's replicate-first, erasure-code-later design. And every one commits a write by recording it in the metadata layer last, after the data is durable.

quiz.q: Why do large object stores erasure code data only after it is sealed?
quiz.a: Sealed data is immutable, so parity is computed once. Hot, still-changing data stays replicated where writes are simpler and faster.

title: Facebook 2010: 260 billion photos drowning in metadata I/O
body: In 2010, Facebook stored over 260 billion images, more than 20 PB, took in about one billion new photos, roughly 60 TB, per week, and served over one million images per second at peak. Each upload was stored in four sizes. The first design used NAS appliances over NFS, with one file per image. The bottleneck was metadata I/O: reading one photo took several disk operations just to find it, so disk seeks, not bandwidth, limited performance.
deeper: Reading one photo on the NFS design meant one or more disk operations to translate the filename to an inode, one to read the inode, and one to read the data itself. With a naive directory layout, a single read could take more than 10 disk operations. Since each hard drive offers only on the order of 120 random operations per second, spending most of them on filesystem bookkeeping rather than photo bytes wasted the scarcest resource. The problem compounds with the four stored sizes per upload, because each size is another file with its own inode and directory entry. Caching metadata in memory helps only if it fits, and with hundreds of billions of files, general-purpose filesystem metadata was far too large to keep fully in RAM. Meta's photo story, from this starting point to Haystack, then f4, then Tectonic, is the best public example of one company evolving object storage over a decade. Its first step, Haystack, was published at OSDI 2010 and attacked exactly this metadata overhead.

quiz.q: Why was Facebook's NFS photo store limited by disk seeks, not bandwidth?
quiz.a: Each read needed several disk operations for directory lookup, inode and data. Seeks for metadata, not bandwidth, used up each drive's limited I/O.

title: Haystack: photos as needles, one disk read per photo
body: Haystack, published at OSDI 2010, packed many photos into a few very large files called physical volumes, about 100 GB each. Each photo is a needle inside a volume, consisting of a header, a key, flags, size, the data and a checksum. Each Store machine keeps an in-memory index from photo key to volume, offset and size. So a read needs at most one disk operation: seek to the offset and read. The filesystem metadata overhead disappears.
deeper: The design works because the in-memory index is tiny compared with general filesystem metadata: just a key and a few numbers per photo, rather than inodes, directory entries and permissions. That made it feasible to hold the whole map in RAM, removing every metadata disk operation from the read path. Writes are appends to the end of a volume, which suits hard drives well. An update is just a new needle with the same key; the newest one wins. Deletes set a flag in the needle, and compaction later rewrites volumes to reclaim space from deleted and overwritten needles. For fast recovery, each volume has an index file so a machine can rebuild its in-memory map quickly after a restart, rather than scanning 100 GB volumes. Above the Store machines, a Directory maps logical volumes to physical volumes on different machines, which provides replication, and a Cache absorbs hot reads. The paper reports each usable terabyte cost about 28% less and served about 4x more reads per second than the NAS setup.

quiz.q: What did Haystack change to cut disk operations per photo read?
quiz.a: It packed photos into large volume files and kept an in-memory key-to-offset index, so a read takes at most one disk operation instead of several.

title: f4's insight: request rates collapse as photos age
body: Haystack kept three replicas, and each Store machine used RAID-6, giving an effective replication factor of 3.6, or 3 x 1.2. That was fine for hot data but too expensive for data nobody reads. Meta measured that BLOB request rates fall sharply with age: week-old BLOBs had an order of magnitude lower request rate than content less than a day old, for eight of nine types studied. Photos became warm after about three months, and profile photos were never moved.
deeper: This measurement is the real innovation of f4, published at OSDI 2014. A BLOB is a binary large object, such as a photo or video. If requests drop by an order of magnitude within a week, then the vast majority of stored bytes are rarely read, yet under Haystack they paid for 3.6x raw storage and the I/O capacity designed for hot traffic. The measurement justified a separate warm tier: once content cools, it can move to a system optimized for low cost per byte rather than high I/O per byte. The rule was not uniform. Photos were considered warm after about three months, while profile photos, which stay popular because they appear everywhere a user does, were never moved. The chapter's senior staff lens stresses the point: f4 did not win by a clever code, it won by measuring access by age and building a cheaper tier for the long tail. Before designing any storage tier, get the request-rate-by-object-age curve for your own data. S3 lifecycle rules apply the same insight.

quiz.q: Where does Haystack's 3.6x effective replication factor come from?
quiz.a: Three replicas, each on a Store machine using RAID-6 with 1.2x overhead: 3 x 1.2 = 3.6x raw storage per logical byte.

title: f4 in a cell: Reed-Solomon 10+4 across racks
body: f4 stores warm BLOBs more cheaply than Haystack. Inside a cell, data is encoded with Reed-Solomon (10,4): 10 data blocks plus 4 parity blocks, so any 10 of the 14 can rebuild the data. That is a storage overhead of 1.4x, compared with 3.6x for Haystack. The blocks of each stripe are spread across racks, so losing a whole rack removes at most a small number of blocks from any stripe. In 2014, f4 stored over 65 PB of logical data.
deeper: Erasure coding suits warm data particularly well. Reads are rare, so the extra work of reconstruction when a block is missing matters little, while the capacity savings apply to every stored byte. And because f4 holds data that has already cooled, it is effectively immutable: no small in-place updates force parity recomputation. Spreading a stripe's blocks across racks applies the same placement logic S3 uses across drives, hosts and Availability Zones. A rack can fail as a unit, due to a switch or power problem, and if several blocks of one stripe sat in that rack, a single failure could take out more than the four the code tolerates. Rack-aware placement keeps failures close to independent. The 1.4x overhead applies within one cell, in one region. Protecting against the loss of an entire region needs another layer. Keeping a second full encoded copy in another region would double overhead to 2.8x; f4 instead used a cheaper XOR scheme across regions, described on the next card, which brought the effective factor to 2.1x.

quiz.q: Why is erasure coding a good fit for warm data specifically?
quiz.a: Warm data is rarely read and effectively immutable, so reconstruction cost is rarely paid and parity never needs updating, while capacity savings apply to every byte.

title: f4's XOR trick: survive a region loss at 2.1x, not 2.8x
body: To survive losing a whole region, f4 did not store a full second copy. Instead it paired two volumes in two different regions, and stored their XOR in a third region. If any one region is lost, its volume can be rebuilt from its buddy volume and the XOR. Two full encoded copies would cost 1.4 x 2 = 2.8x. With XOR geo-replication, it is (1.4 x 2 + 1.4) / 2 = 2.1x per logical byte.
deeper: XOR is the simplest possible parity: A XOR B stored separately means that if A is lost, A equals B XOR (A XOR B), and vice versa. Applied to whole volumes across regions, it acts as a geographically distributed erasure code with two data pieces and one parity piece. The accounting works out as follows. Volume A in region A is stored at 1.4x because of Reed-Solomon (10,4) within its cell. Buddy volume B in region B is also 1.4x. The XOR volume in region C is the same size as one volume and also encoded at 1.4x. Total raw storage is 1.4 + 1.4 + 1.4 = 4.2 for two logical volumes, which is 2.1x per logical byte. Compare 2.8x for keeping two full encoded copies and 3.6x for Haystack. The trade-off is recovery cost: rebuilding after a region loss requires reading both the buddy and the XOR from other regions, which is heavy on cross-region bandwidth. For warm, rarely read data, that rare expense is worth the large permanent savings.

quiz.q: Explain Meta's effective replication factors of 3.6x, 2.8x and 2.1x.
quiz.a: Haystack: 3 replicas x RAID-6 1.2 = 3.6x. f4 RS(10,4) is 1.4x; two regional copies give 2.8x. XOR geo-replication: (1.4+1.4+1.4)/2 = 2.1x.

title: Measure access by age: f4 saved about 97 PB of disk
body: A back-of-envelope estimate: at 65 PB of logical data, moving from Haystack's 3.6x to f4's 2.1x saves 65 x 1.5, about 97 PB of raw disk. That is the kind of number that pays for a whole storage team. The senior staff lens: f4 did not win with a clever code. It won by measuring access by age and building a cheaper tier for the long tail. Before designing a storage tier, get the request rate by object age curve for your data.
deeper: The lesson is about where engineering leverage comes from. Reed-Solomon codes and XOR parity were well known long before f4. What made the project valuable was the measurement that most BLOBs cool dramatically within days or weeks, combined with the decision to act on it with a separate system tuned for cold bytes. The saving scales with data size, so at Meta's scale the difference of 1.5x per logical byte turned into tens of petabytes of disks, plus the servers, power, space and operations to run them. For your own systems, the request-rate-by-age curve tells you whether a tier is worth building and where the threshold belongs. If requests fall steeply after a week, tiering can save a great deal; if access is flat or unpredictable, a warm tier may cost more in retrieval and complexity than it saves. The same curve informs S3 lifecycle rules, such as moving photos older than 90 days to a cheaper class while keeping profile photos hot, the same exception Meta made.

quiz.q: What was the real reason f4 succeeded, according to the chapter?
quiz.a: Measuring how request rates fall with object age and building a cheaper tier for the rarely read long tail, not a novel coding scheme.

title: Tectonic: one exabyte filesystem to stop stranding resources
body: By 2021, Meta had replaced Haystack, f4 and its data-warehouse HDFS clusters with Tectonic, an exabyte-scale multitenant filesystem described at FAST 2021. The reason: specialized systems strand resources. Haystack ran out of IOPS while capacity sat spare, and f4 ran out of capacity while IOPS sat spare. One shared system can use both. Tectonic scales a single cluster to exabytes, one per datacenter, serving about ten tenants such as blob storage and the data warehouse.
deeper: Stranding is an efficiency problem that specialization creates. Each specialized system is sized for its own bottleneck, so its other resource is left over and cannot be lent to anyone else. Hot photo storage needs I/O and has room to spare; warm storage needs capacity and has idle I/O. Put both tenants on the same drives and the hot tenant uses the I/O while the cold tenant uses the capacity, mixing hot and cold bytes per drive, which is the same goal S3 pursues with rebalancing. Tectonic's metadata design makes that scale possible. It splits metadata into independently scalable layers, Name, File and Block, stored in ZippyDB, and uses hash partitioning to avoid metadata hotspots, avoiding the key-range hotspot problem that S3 users must manage with key design. Each tenant can choose its own encoding, for example RS(9,6) for long-lived data, so consolidation does not force one durability trade-off on everyone. Moving the data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10x.

quiz.q: Why did consolidating Haystack and f4 into Tectonic improve efficiency?
quiz.a: Each stranded one resource: Haystack spare capacity, f4 spare IOPS. A shared system lets hot tenants use I/O and cold tenants use capacity on the same drives.

title: Haystack to f4 to Tectonic: specialize, specialize, merge
body: Meta's decade of photo storage follows a clear arc. Haystack specialized for performance, cutting disk operations per read to at most one. f4 specialized again for cost, moving cooled data to an erasure-coded warm tier at 2.1x instead of 3.6x. Tectonic then consolidated everything, including the data warehouse, into one multitenant filesystem for efficiency and simpler operations. Each step solved the previous design's main weakness: first I/O, then storage cost, then stranded resources.
deeper: The arc is a useful template for thinking about any storage platform's lifecycle. Early on, one workload dominates and a specialized system tuned for its bottleneck wins big, as Haystack did with 4x more reads per second than NAS. As data accumulates and cools, cost becomes the dominant problem, and a second specialized tier pays off, as f4 did with roughly 97 PB of raw disk saved. But multiple specialized systems each strand resources and each need their own operations team, tooling and capacity planning. Eventually the overhead of running several systems outweighs the gains of specialization, and a general, multitenant system with per-tenant choices becomes the better design. Tectonic kept the benefits of specialization through per-tenant encoding choices, such as RS(9,6) for long-lived data, while pooling I/O and capacity. The chapter's key takeaways summarize the three strategies: optimize for I/O, then for cost using age-based tiers, then consolidate to stop stranding resources. The comparison is also a caution against assuming the current design is final.

quiz.q: What problem did each step of Meta's Haystack, f4, Tectonic arc solve?
quiz.a: Haystack cut read I/O, f4 cut storage cost for cooled data with erasure coding, and Tectonic consolidated systems to stop stranding IOPS and capacity.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
title: Dropbox left S3: 500 PB moved to Magic Pocket by 2015
body: Dropbox originally stored its users' file blocks on Amazon S3. The Magic Pocket project began in 2013, and by October 2015 Dropbox served over 90% of user data from its own infrastructure, after moving over 500 PB. Dropbox gave two reasons: end-to-end control over performance, and better unit economics at its scale. It is the classic example of a company leaving the public cloud for its core storage.
deeper: Moving 500 PB is a multi-year engineering effort, not a configuration change, and it only makes sense when the benefits are large and durable. Control over performance means Dropbox could tune the whole path, hardware, network and software, for its own workload rather than for the average S3 customer. Unit economics means that at hundreds of petabytes, the margin a cloud provider charges on each byte becomes large enough to fund building and running your own storage, including the team. The chapter's in-industry note explains why it worked for Dropbox specifically: the workload is simple, since blocks are immutable; huge, at hundreds of petabytes; and predictable, growing steadily rather than spiking. It warns that the same decision would be poor for a company with small or spiky storage needs. Such a company would lose the decorrelation benefit of S3, where millions of workloads with unaligned peaks share one fleet, and would also have to staff a storage team to handle durability, repair and hardware lifecycle that S3 otherwise provides.

quiz.q: Why would leaving S3 be a poor choice for a company with small, spiky storage needs?
quiz.a: It loses S3's decorrelation benefit of sharing a smoothed fleet, and must staff a storage team, without the scale that made Dropbox's economics work.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
title: Inside Magic Pocket: 4 MB blocks, 1 GB buckets, 50 PB cells
body: Dropbox's 2016 description of Magic Pocket: files are cut into blocks of up to 4 MB. Blocks are grouped into 1 GB buckets, which are stored in volumes that are replicated or erasure coded across storage machines. A cell holds about 50 PB raw. Each block is stored in at least two geographic zones, with cross-zone replication within about one second of upload. New data is replicated first, then erasure coded later for efficiency.
deeper: The block-and-bucket hierarchy is another instance of packing small things into big immutable containers, like Haystack's needles in 100 GB volumes. Tracking billions of 4 MB blocks individually on disk would multiply metadata; grouping them into 1 GB buckets lets storage machines deal with a manageable number of large units. Replicating new data first and erasure coding it later matches the seal-then-encode pattern seen at Azure and in Meta's Haystack-to-f4 path: fresh data is replicated for simple, fast writes and reads, then converted to a cheaper encoding once it settles. Storing each block in at least two geographic zones, replicated within about one second, protects against losing a site while keeping the window of single-zone exposure short. One distinctive choice is coordination. Each cell has a simple central Master rather than a Paxos-based coordinator, the consensus approach many distributed systems use for fault-tolerant coordination. Dropbox chose simplicity wherever it could, accepting a simpler central component over the complexity of consensus. The comparison table lists Magic Pocket's metadata as a per-cell Master plus a block index.

quiz.q: Why does Magic Pocket replicate new data first and erasure code it later?
quiz.a: Replication gives simple, fast handling of fresh data; once data settles, erasure coding reduces storage overhead, the same seal-then-encode pattern as Azure and f4.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
title: SMR drives: terrible for filesystems, perfect for Dropbox
body: In 2018, Dropbox deployed SMR, or shingled magnetic recording, drives at petabyte scale. SMR drives overlap their tracks like roof shingles, which packs in more data but means you cannot rewrite a small region in place without disturbing neighboring tracks. That makes them a poor fit for most filesystems, which do many small in-place updates. But Magic Pocket's extents are append-only and immutable, written in large sequential chunks, a perfect match. With 14 TB SMR drives, one chassis reached about 1.4 PB.
deeper: SMR is a good illustration of how design decisions made years earlier unlock hardware choices later. Because Magic Pocket was built around immutable blocks and append-only extents, it never needed to rewrite small regions, so the main drawback of shingled recording simply did not apply. A general-purpose filesystem, by contrast, constantly updates metadata and file contents in place, which on SMR would require rewriting large zones for each small change, destroying performance. The payoff is density: SMR drives store more per drive, which lowers cost per byte, and in Dropbox's deployment one chassis of 14 TB drives reached about 1.4 PB. This connects to the heat discussion earlier in the chapter. Denser drives make I/O per terabyte even scarcer, so they suit data that is written once, read occasionally and rarely rewritten, exactly the profile of most synced file blocks. The broader lesson is that immutability is not just a software convenience; it widens the range of cheap hardware a storage system can use.

quiz.q: Why were SMR drives a good fit for Dropbox but a poor fit for a general filesystem?
quiz.a: SMR cannot rewrite small regions in place. Magic Pocket writes large append-only immutable extents; general filesystems do many small in-place updates.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
title: Backblaze Vaults: 17+3 across 20 pods for 1.18x overhead
body: Backblaze publishes its storage design openly. A Vault is 20 Storage Pods. Each file is split into 17 data shards plus 3 parity shards, with one shard on each pod. Drives in the same position across the 20 pods form a tome, and each file lives in one tome. A Vault survives up to three drive losses in a tome, or three pods offline. Overhead is 20 / 17, about 1.18x. With 20 TB drives, one Vault holds about 20.2 PB.
deeper: Backblaze's very low overhead is the result of explicit choices. Wide stripes, 17 data shards for only 3 parity, keep the parity fraction small; compare Meta f4's 1.4x or the illustrative 1.5x needed to survive an Availability Zone loss at S3. Backblaze runs each vault in a single site, so there is no multi-AZ spread inside a vault that would require extra parity to survive a zone failure. And it uses cheap commodity pods rather than specialized hardware. The tome structure makes placement simple and failure domains clear: a file's 20 shards sit on the same drive slot across 20 pods, so each pod holds exactly one shard and any three pods can be offline for maintenance or failure without losing data. The trade-off is what a single-site design gives up. A disaster affecting the site affects the whole vault, and wide stripes mean rebuilding a lost shard requires reading from many pods. The comparison table summarizes Backblaze's main idea in three words: wide cheap stripes.

quiz.q: Why can Backblaze reach 1.18x overhead when S3-style multi-AZ designs need more?
quiz.a: It uses very wide 17+3 stripes in a single site, with no need for extra parity to survive losing a whole zone, on cheap commodity pods.

section: 3.6 Open source: MinIO and Ceph RGW
title: MinIO: erasure sets, quorums, and no metadata database
body: MinIO is an S3-compatible object server. Drives are grouped into erasure sets, by default 2 to 16 drives, and each object is Reed-Solomon coded across one set. With 16 drives, the default parity is EC:4, giving 75% usable capacity and tolerating 4 drive failures. Reads need a quorum of K healthy drives. Writes need K, or K+1 when parity is exactly half the set, to avoid split-brain, where two groups each believe they hold the latest data.
deeper: K here is the number of data shards: with 16 drives and EC:4 parity, K is 12, so 12 of 16 drives must be healthy to read. Write quorum is normally also K, but when parity equals half the set, two disjoint halves of equal size could each accept conflicting writes, so MinIO requires K+1 to guarantee that any two write quorums overlap. MinIO's most distinctive choice is having no separate metadata database. Object metadata travels with the object, stored on the same drives. That keeps the system simple: there is no index service to scale, back up or keep consistent with the data. The cost shows up in listing and metadata-heavy operations, which must gather information from the drives themselves and so are more expensive than in systems with a dedicated index, like S3's sharded index layer or Ceph's bucket index. The comparison table summarizes MinIO as RS per erasure set, for example EC:4, with metadata stored with the object, and a main idea of simple, no metadata DB.

quiz.q: What does MinIO gain and lose by storing metadata with each object?
quiz.a: It gains simplicity with no separate index service, but listing and metadata-heavy operations become more expensive than in systems with a dedicated index.

section: 3.6 Open source: MinIO and Ceph RGW
title: Ceph RGW: S3 on RADOS, and the bucket-index trap
body: Ceph's RADOS Gateway, or RGW, exposes S3 and Swift APIs on top of RADOS, Ceph's distributed object layer. Objects are placed with the CRUSH algorithm, covered in Chapter 2. Bucket listings rely on a bucket index stored in RADOS objects. For big buckets that index must be sharded, and Ceph supports dynamic resharding. Unsharded or under-sharded bucket indexes are a well-known cause of slow writes on large RGW buckets. Multisite configuration replicates data between clusters.
deeper: RGW illustrates the metadata-over-data pattern in open-source form: RADOS stores bytes, and a separate bucket index tracks which objects exist in each bucket so listings work. The index itself lives in RADOS objects, and every write to a bucket must update it. If one index object covers a huge bucket, it becomes a hotspot that every write must touch, and write performance drops as the bucket grows. Sharding spreads the index over many RADOS objects so updates can proceed in parallel. Dynamic resharding lets Ceph split the index as the bucket grows, similar in spirit to S3 splitting index partitions under load. Knowing this failure mode is practical operations knowledge: when a large RGW bucket suddenly slows down on writes, the bucket index sharding is a prime suspect. Placement with CRUSH means clients can compute where objects live rather than asking a central table, which removes a lookup service from the data path. Data protection comes from replication or erasure coding within RADOS, as the comparison table notes, and the main design idea is S3 API on a general object layer.

quiz.q: Why do large Ceph RGW buckets get slow writes when their index is unsharded?
quiz.a: Every write updates the bucket index; one index object becomes a hotspot. Sharding the index spreads those updates across many RADOS objects.

section: 3.6 Open source: MinIO and Ceph RGW
title: Common mistake: S3-compatible does not mean behaves like S3
body: A common mistake is assuming that a system advertised as S3-compatible behaves like Amazon S3. Compatibility usually means the same API calls work, not that the same guarantees hold. Consistency on overwrite and listing, request-rate scaling, listing performance on huge buckets, and support for newer APIs such as conditional writes and additional checksums all vary between implementations. The only safe approach is to test your real workload on the system you plan to use.
deeper: Each of those areas maps to something the chapter showed is hard. S3 took 14 years and a verified cache coherence protocol to offer strong consistency for all GET, PUT, LIST and DELETE operations; another system might accept the same requests but return stale reads after an overwrite. S3 scales request rates by splitting index partitions per prefix; another system may have a fixed limit or a single hot index, like an under-sharded Ceph RGW bucket index. Listing speed depends on how metadata is stored: MinIO keeps metadata with objects, which is simpler but makes listing and metadata-heavy operations costlier than with a dedicated index. Newer features such as conditional writes, added to S3 in 2024, are precisely what table formats and lock-free coordination protocols rely on for atomic create-if-absent steps. If a compatible system silently ignores an If-None-Match header, a commit protocol built on it could corrupt data without raising any error. Testing should therefore cover the actual guarantees your application depends on, including concurrency and failure cases, not just whether basic uploads and downloads succeed.

quiz.q: Why is missing conditional-write support in an S3-compatible store dangerous?
quiz.a: Table formats rely on If-None-Match for atomic commits. If the header is ignored, concurrent writers can overwrite each other without any error.

title: Data protection compared: from 3.6x replicas to 1.18x stripes
body: The chapter's comparison table shows how differently each system protects data. S3 uses Reed-Solomon across 3 or more Availability Zones with an 11 nines design. Azure uses synchronous replicas in a stamp, erasure codes sealed extents, and replicates asynchronously across regions. Meta Haystack used 3 replicas plus RAID-6 at 3.6x; f4 used RS(10,4) plus XOR across regions at 2.1x; Tectonic uses per-tenant RS, such as RS(9,6). Backblaze uses 17+3 across 20 pods at 1.18x.
deeper: The remaining rows complete the picture. Google Cloud Storage relies on Colossus encodings, chosen per application by the Colossus client library. Dropbox Magic Pocket replicates first and then erasure codes, across 2 or more zones. MinIO uses Reed-Solomon per erasure set, for example EC:4. Ceph RGW uses replication or erasure coding within RADOS. Reading these side by side reveals the main levers. Overhead falls as stripes widen, from Haystack's 3.6x replication to Backblaze's 1.18x wide stripes. Overhead rises with the size of the failure you insist on surviving: a design meant to lose an entire Availability Zone or region needs more parity or cross-region schemes, while a single-site design like a Backblaze vault can use thin parity. Most systems also change protection as data ages: replicate while hot, erasure code once sealed or cooled, as with Azure, Magic Pocket and Meta's Haystack-to-f4 move. The public year column adds context: S3 from 2006, Google Cloud Storage from 2010, the Azure WAS paper from 2011, Haystack 2010, f4 2014, Tectonic 2021, Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vault 2015, and MinIO and Ceph RGW as open source.

quiz.q: Why can a Backblaze vault run at 1.18x while S3 needs more overhead?
quiz.a: Backblaze uses wide stripes in a single site. S3 spreads shards across at least three AZs and must survive losing a whole zone, which demands more parity.

title: Metadata compared: where each system keeps its index
body: Every system in the chapter answers the question of where metadata lives differently. S3 uses its own sharded index plus witness-based cache coherence. Google Cloud Storage uses Spanner for permissions and location, and Bigtable for Colossus metadata. Azure uses a partition layer with range partitions. Haystack kept an in-memory needle index per machine. Tectonic uses ZippyDB, layered and hash partitioned. Magic Pocket uses a per-cell Master plus a block index. MinIO stores metadata with the object. Ceph RGW keeps a bucket index in RADOS.
deeper: The main design idea column pairs with these metadata choices. S3: massive multitenancy, heat spread and formal checks with ShardStore. Google Cloud Storage: shared Google infrastructure and strong global consistency. Azure: stamps and an append-only stream layer. Haystack: one disk I/O per read. f4: a warm tier by object age, with metadata separate from Haystack. Tectonic: consolidate all tenants. Magic Pocket: immutable 4 MB blocks and SMR drives. Backblaze: wide cheap stripes with a tome-based layout. MinIO: simple, no metadata database. Ceph RGW: the S3 API on a general object layer. The metadata choice largely determines what is easy and what is hard. A dedicated, partitioned index, as in S3, Azure and Tectonic, makes listing and consistency tractable but must be scaled and protected from hotspots; S3 partitions by key range, Tectonic hashes to avoid hotspots. A globally consistent database like Spanner makes strong consistency natural. Keeping metadata with the object, like MinIO, is simplest but makes listing costly. An under-sharded index, like an RGW bucket index, becomes a write bottleneck.

quiz.q: What trade-off does a dedicated metadata index make compared with MinIO's approach?
quiz.a: A dedicated index makes listing and consistency efficient but must be scaled and kept free of hotspots; storing metadata with objects is simpler but makes listing expensive.

title: Takeaways: immutability, index-last commits, verified code
body: Object storage rests on immutable objects in a flat namespace. Immutability makes caching, replication and erasure coding simple, and makes in-place updates impossible. Every large object store separates a metadata or index layer from an append-only data layer, and commits a write by writing the index entry last. S3 reached strong consistency in 2020 using a witness as a read barrier, backed by proofs and model checking. ShardStore shows lightweight formal methods can be maintained by normal engineers and catch real crash bugs.
deeper: These four ideas connect. Immutability is what makes the metadata-over-data split work: because data never changes after it is written, the data layer can be simple append-only storage and apply erasure coding once, while all coordination is concentrated in the index. Writing data first and the index entry last turns the index into the commit point, so a crash leaves only unreferenced garbage rather than a visible object with missing bytes. The same index layer is where consistency is decided, which is why S3's 2020 upgrade focused on keeping its metadata cache coherent: a small, in-memory witness tells caches when their view is stale, and AWS verified the protocol with deductive proofs and model checking, with verification effort exceeding implementation. ShardStore applies the same rigor to the storage node itself: an executable reference model about 1% of the code size, property-based testing with random crashes and disk failures, and model checking of concurrency, which prevented 16 issues from reaching production. Together they explain how a system built from failing parts can make strong promises.

quiz.q: Why does writing the index entry last make it the commit point?
quiz.a: Readers only find objects through the index. If data is durable before the entry exists, a crash leaves only invisible garbage, never a visible object with missing bytes.

title: Takeaways: 11 nines, heat, prefixes, tiers, moving up the stack
body: Eleven nines comes from erasure coding across Availability Zones, fast detection and repair, and processes like durability reviews that guard against software and human error. On hard drives, the scarce resource is I/O per byte, called heat, not capacity; S3 manages it with wide placement and workload decorrelation. S3 scales per prefix, so spread hot keys and retry 503s. Meta's Haystack, f4, Tectonic path shows three strategies. And object storage keeps moving up the stack.
deeper: Each takeaway has a practical design-review question. On durability: beyond the coding scheme, how fast is repair, and what protects against bad deploys, garbage-collection bugs and operator mistakes, such as versioning, delayed deletion and formal checks? On heat: since a drive does about 120 random I/Os per second regardless of capacity, how will hot data be spread so no drive becomes a tail-latency hotspot? On request rates: S3 supports at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per partitioned prefix, so does the key design spread load, or does a date-first prefix funnel everything into one partition? On tiering: what does the request-rate-by-age curve look like, and does it justify a cheaper tier, as it did for f4, where measuring access by age cut effective replication from 3.6x to 2.1x before Tectonic consolidated tenants to stop stranding resources? On the future: with S3 Express One Zone for low latency, S3 Tables for native Iceberg and S3 Vectors for embeddings, will object storage absorb the specialized system you are about to build?

quiz.q: Why is I/O per byte, not capacity, the scarce resource on hard-drive fleets?
quiz.a: Drive capacity keeps growing while random I/O stays near 120 per second, so each terabyte gets less I/O every year.
